IMRP exploratory data analysis and year-selection recommendation

Local snapshot analysed: 30 June 2016 to 12 July 2026 | Generated from C:\Users\jamie\GitHub\PhD\Data_Centre\static\data\imrp_actuals.csv

Recommendation for the paper revision

Use calendar year 2025 as the primary empirical price year if one year must be selected. It is complete, recent, post-dates the 2021–22 high-price regime, and is the closest of the three most recent complete years (2023–2025) to their multivariate median across price level, spread, tails, negative-price frequency, high-price frequency, hourly ramps, seasonality, and intraday shape.

For a defensible paper, do not present 2025 as universally representative of 2016–2026. State that it is a recent-regime representative year selected by a pre-specified score. Use 2023 and 2024 as recent-year sensitivity cases, and use 2022 only as a deliberate high-price stress case. If computationally feasible, the stronger design is to run every valid day in 2025 and report the distribution of model outcomes rather than one hand-picked 24-hour day.

Central finding. The dataset is structurally complete but not statistically stationary. Annual median, dispersion, negative-price incidence, and extreme-price frequency change markedly across the record. A single year can support a bounded case study, but it cannot substitute for temporal sensitivity analysis.

1. What this dataset represents

The column name IMRP means Intermittent Market Reference Price. According to the Low Carbon Contracts Company (LCCC), it is the GB day-ahead hourly price calculated as a weighted average across day-ahead indices. The portal defines IMRP_Amount in £/MWh, the settlement date as the date on which the price applies, and settlement period 1 as the first hourly period of the day. See the official LCCC dataset description and market-reference-price methodology page.

This is a good conceptual match for the paper's day-ahead price input. It is not an imbalance price, consumer retail tariff, or a site-specific electricity bill. In the revision, call it an LCCC GB day-ahead Intermittent Market Reference Price and cite the dataset version/date.

2. Data-quality and coverage audit

  • No missing settlement dates: 0 dates are absent from the continuous range.
  • No null cells: 0 null values occur in the three source columns.
  • No duplicate date-period keys: 0 duplicates were found.
  • Daylight saving is represented: daily counts range from 23 to 25 hourly periods. This is expected for 23- and 25-hour clock-change days and should not be repaired by deleting or duplicating observations.
  • Partial edge years: 2016 and 2026 are incomplete calendar years and were excluded from like-for-like calendar-year ranking. All 87,960 observations remain included in the long-run descriptive analysis.

3. What changes across years

The annual mean is consistently above the median in the high-price years, showing strong right-skew from price spikes. The central distribution, upper tail, negative-price incidence, and within-day hourly changes all vary materially. Therefore, selecting a year based only on the annual mean would omit behaviour that directly determines the value of workload shifting and storage arbitrage.

The score is a weighted robust distance from the 2023–2025 median using: median (20%), IQR (15%), 5th percentile (10%), 95th percentile (15%), negative-hour share (10%), share above £200/MWh (10%), 95th-percentile hourly ramp (10%), monthly amplitude (5%), and intraday amplitude (5%). Lower is more representative of the recent regime.

4. Seasonal and intraday structure

Both seasonal price levels and the shape of the median day change between years. These dimensions matter for a data-centre model: storage and deferred workload respond to within-day spreads, while annual cost and available arbitrage opportunities depend on how frequently those daily shapes occur.

5. Comparing selection strategies

Calendar year

Recommended for the paper. It has an intuitive January–December boundary, preserves all seasons, is easy to cite and reproduce, and aligns with annual reporting. Complete candidates are 2017–2025.

First-timestep-anchored year

Useful for the overlay requested earlier, but the 30 June boundary is arbitrary for a paper. The rolling-year median closest to the rolling-window median is 2018–19; this answer differs because changing the boundary reallocates winter and crisis months.

Latest complete year

Simple and current, but not automatically representative. It should be chosen only if the paper's claim is explicitly about the latest observed market conditions. Here, the latest complete calendar year is 2025.

Random or visually selected year

Not recommended. It is hard to defend and creates a cherry-picking concern because the model's savings are highly sensitive to price spread and extreme events.

Why 2025 is the best primary choice

  1. Completeness: 8,760 hourly observations across 365 settlement dates, including the leap-year and daylight-saving structure.
  2. Recency without using an incomplete year: it belongs to the latest three fully observed calendar years.
  3. Transparent representativeness: it ranks 1 among the recent candidates by the stated recent-regime score (0.05).
  4. Neither a crisis peak nor a deliberately calm year: its median is £81.3/MWh, IQR is £25.8/MWh, negative-price share is 1.92%, and 95th percentile is £122.9/MWh.
  5. Clear academic framing: it can be described as a recent representative year, while 2023 and 2024 provide recent-year robustness checks and 2022 provides a high-price stress test.

The typical day is selected by minimising a robust distance to the year's median 24-hour shape and daily level/spread features, using only 24-period days. Clock-change days are excluded from this daily-profile step because they do not fit a fixed 24-hour model horizon. The volatility and high-price cases are chosen near the 90th percentile rather than at the absolute maximum, while the negative-price case deliberately tests the sign reversal that the present paper profile cannot represent.

7. Implications for the current 24-hour paper model

Do not create a single "average day" and treat it as representative. Averaging each hour across a year smooths spikes, negative prices, and day-to-day covariation. Those are precisely the features that create value for UPS/TES dispatch and workload shifting.

The present paper profile has mean £86.9/MWh, median £90.0/MWh, range £92.0/MWh, standard deviation £29.2/MWh, and a 95th-percentile hourly ramp of £15.0/MWh. It is a smooth, entirely positive constructed profile. It is useful pedagogically but does not reproduce the empirical distribution of negative prices, spikes, or irregular daily shapes.

Preferred revision design

  1. Primary dataset: use all valid days in calendar year 2025.
  2. Simulation unit: retain the 24-hour optimisation horizon, but run it separately for every 24-period day (with the same 3-hour extension logic drawn from the following day where available).
  3. Clock changes: pre-specify treatment of the one 23-period and one 25-period day. The cleanest approach for a fixed 24-hour model is to exclude those two dates from the daily runs while retaining them in annual descriptive statistics.
  4. Reported outcome: report the median, interquartile range, and 5th–95th percentile of cost saving and flexibility metrics across days, not only the result from one day.
  5. Robustness: repeat the annual analysis for 2023 and 2024; add 2022 as an explicit stress regime. If computational cost is prohibitive, use the four objectively selected 2025 profiles above and label the design as representative-day sampling.
  6. Claims: limit conclusions to the observed GB day-ahead reference-price conditions and avoid claiming that one year represents all market regimes.

8. Limitations and cautions

  • The selection score operationalises "representative" for a recent GB day-ahead regime. A historical-study, stress-test, or latest-market objective would justify a different year.
  • Prices are nominal £/MWh. Comparing price levels across a decade does not adjust for inflation; the report therefore emphasises within-year distribution and shape as well as level.
  • The dataset supplies the market reference signal, not network constraints, site tariffs, imbalance exposure, or demand charges.
  • Extreme observations were retained. They are economically relevant for flexibility, but the report does not independently validate each extreme against a second market-data source.
  • Daily representative profiles are a computational compromise. Full-year repeated optimisation is preferable whenever practical.
